name: Garlic gel

lead: Garlic gel is a home remedy rubbed onto the scalp for alopecia areata, an autoimmune cause of patchy hair loss, with the aim of regrowing hair in bald spots.

Proponents say it stimulates the scalp and may calm local immune activity, though no mechanism has been established in the sources available. The only registered trial found was a small phase 3 study of a topical garlic concentrate in children that began in 2016 and was terminated after eight participants, with no results posted.

paras: It is discussed in non-prescription regrowth contexts and applied as a gel or preparation to patches of hair loss. It is used alongside or instead of standard alopecia areata treatments.
Raw garlic applied to skin has been reported to cause burns, and references advise caution, especially in young children. It is not an approved treatment for alopecia areata.

angle.text: Garlic gel is a folk remedy applied to bald patches in alopecia areata, with the hope of regrowth in those spots. One children's trial was registered and terminated after eight participants; raw garlic has caused skin burns.

lead: Garlic gel is a topical preparation made from garlic (Allium sativum) that has been used as a folk or alternative approach to hair regrowth, mainly in alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition that causes patchy hair loss. People apply it to bald patches hoping to see hair return, which would restore a fuller hairline or scalp.

A 2007 double-blind randomized trial of 40 patients with localized alopecia areata combined topical garlic gel or placebo with betamethasone cream twice daily for three months; good or moderate responses were seen in 19 of 20 garlic-treated patients, significantly better than the placebo group, with no complications reported [1]. A 2014 evidence-based review of randomized alopecia areata trials listed garlic gel among a miscellaneous group of topical treatments with less scientific evidence [2].

A phase 3 registered trial of a topical garlic concentrate in children with alopecia areata began in January 2016, enrolled eight participants and was terminated, with no results listed [3]. A 2023 review in Cutis examined the evidence behind topical hair-loss remedies popular on TikTok, naming garlic gel along with rosemary oil, rice water and onion juice [4]. Raw garlic applied to skin has been reported to cause burns [5].
infobox: Not an approved treatment for hair loss

paras: Garlic gel and garlic extracts are applied to the scalp by some people with patchy hair loss, in the belief that garlic stimulates regrowth. The condition most associated with it is alopecia areata, in which the immune system attacks hair follicles [2]. Garlic gel is also named among natural remedies promoted for hair loss on social media [4].

The 2014 review of 29 randomized trials in alopecia areata found no universally proven therapy and placed garlic gel in the group of miscellaneous topical and oral treatments with less scientific evidence [2]. The 2007 trial is the randomized study usually cited for garlic gel [1].

General references on garlic note that serious burns have resulted from raw garlic applied to skin, including for naturopathic purposes, and advise caution with topical use on young children [5]. The 2007 trial reported no complications in its patients [1].

A double-blind randomized controlled trial of 40 patients tested garlic gel versus placebo, both with betamethasone valerate cream, for three months in localized alopecia areata; the garlic group had a significantly better response (P = 0.001) [1]. The 2014 review included garlic gel among the miscellaneous treatments assessed [2]. One phase 3 trial in children (NCT02691117) started on 10 January 2016 with eight participants and was terminated; no results are posted [3].

timeline.event: Double-blind randomized trial of garlic gel plus betamethasone cream in localized alopecia areata published in the Indian Journal of Dermatology, Venereology and Leprology [1].

A phase 3 trial of topical garlic concentrate for alopecia areata in children is started (NCT02691117) and later terminated with eight participants [3].
